Article Title: Bill Gates' daughter Phoebe Gates' shopping app Phia is in damage control mode after revelations that 'shocked' many
Article Text:
Phia claimed sales it never drove. Now it is paying brands back

Phia cookie stuffing explained: how fake clicks let a shopping app claim commissions it never earned

Phia calls it a bug, investigation calls it auto_drop: the December 2025 code that ran for seven months

Impact.com suspends Phia as refunds begin, while Phoebe Gates and Sophia Kianni say nothing

Phia, the shopping app co-founded by Phoebe Gates and Sophia Kianni, is now issuing refunds and reversing transactions after admitting it collected commissions on sales it never actually drove. Business Insider reported that the startup is working with affiliate network Impact.com to correct attributions, and a Phia spokesperson confirmed the company has offered transaction reversals to brands. Impact.com said it is reprocessing every action credited to Phia between June 20 and July 29 that had not yet been paid out, reattributing them to the right publisher or refunding advertisers.The cleanup follows a Bloomberg investigation published on July 9 that found Phia's mobile browser extension quietly opening a background tab during checkout and injecting its own referral code, overwriting whoever had actually sent the shopper there. Bloomberg tested the extension across more than 50 retail sites, including Walmart, Nike and Zara. In one test, clicking a Nordstrom link from a Wirecutter article triggered a background tab that swapped Wirecutter's affiliate code for Phia's.The practice has a name in the industry: cookie stuffing, or forced clicks.Affiliate marketing runs on one rule, that a commission is owed only when a user actually clicks a link and then buys. Independent researcher Ben Edelman, who reviewed Phia's public code and ran his own tests, found a setting called enable_coupon_auto_drop that fired affiliate links without any user action, usually at the cart or checkout page. Crucially, it was switched on only for iOS users through a server-side feature flag, which is why desktop-only testers missed it for months.Capital One Shopping, which makes a rival extension, reached the same conclusion and emailed retailers with video evidence. Publishers were losing real revenue, the email said, and advertisers were paying for fake clicks.Phia has called it a bug. Its spokesperson told Bloomberg the company learned that a recent release was causing misattributions from a subset of users, and that the team worked overnight to fix it. Bloomberg retested after contacting the company on July 7 and found the automatic referral claims had stopped.Edelman disputes the framing. The feature first shipped in version 1.9.33 on December 13, 2025, which puts it in the field for roughly seven months, including the holiday shopping season. A feature named auto_drop that automatically drops affiliate cookies, he argues, is hard to describe as an accident.The stakes are high for a company that has raised $43.5 million from Kleiner Perkins, Khosla Ventures and Notable Capital, plus celebrity backers including Hailey Bieber, Khloe Kardashian, Sydney Sweeney and Sheryl Sandberg. Phia's app has been downloaded over 1.2 million times in the past year.Impact.com has temporarily suspended Phia from its marketplace, the tool brands use to find new partners, and wants a stretch of clean compliance before reinstating it. Rakuten Advertising says it is investigating. CJ Affiliate told partners it is making reconciliation payments.Gates and Kianni, who promote Phia constantly across social media and host a podcast called The Burnouts, have said nothing publicly.
Article Summary: Phia's mobile browser extension quietly opened a background tab during checkout and injected its own referral code, overwriting whoever had actually sent the shopper there. Bloomberg tested the extension across more than 50 retail sites, including Walmart, Nike and Zara. The practice has a name in the industry: cookie stuffing, or forced clicks.

Article Title: AI has drawn Google, Meta and other tech companies into construction business, making these jobs one of the highest-paid
Article Text:
Why Google and Meta are spending millions to train electricians

A training centre caught in the middle

The massive appetite for AI’s computing power is turning construction into one of the best-paying trades in the US. Google, Meta and other tech giants are now pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into training the electricians and skilled workers needed to build their data centres, a report has said.For example, one of the data centers being built in Detroit, backed by OpenAI, is being called the single biggest private investment in Michigan's history, as per a report by The New York Times, it needs hundreds of electricians working 10-hour shifts, seven days a week, and it's paying accordingly.The pull of data centre money is the main topic of conversation at the Detroit Electrical Industry Training Center, where roughly 850 apprentices are currently training, the report added. It's one of 270 such centers across the country now getting direct support from AI companies, who are pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into making sure there are enough skilled workers to build their facilities.Meanwhile, Google alone has put in $50 million through a partnership with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, aimed at nearly doubling the union's annual apprenticeship intake from 19,500 to 30,000 over the next three years, at locations Google has picked out itself.Asset management giant BlackRock has chipped in with its own grant as part of a separate $100 million push to widen training pipelines for its data centers in Texas.The report notes that the data centre growth is starting to squeeze everything around it: land and raw materials and workers. According to an analysis by the job site Indeed, hourly installation and maintenance jobs at data centers now pay 42% more than comparable roles in other industries.In hotspots like Dallas and Northern Virginia, where data centre construction is especially dense, workers can jump between projects for bigger bonuses or higher daily rates, and contractors are increasingly turning to staffing agencies like Aerotek just to keep crews fully staffed.Tech companies training their own workforce isn't newThis isn't the first time a tech company has taken on the job of training the people who keep its facilities running. Microsoft has been doing something similar since 2018, when it launched its own data center technician training programs. It now runs 39 such locations worldwide and has trained roughly 15,000 people through them.
Article Summary: Google, Meta and other tech giants are pouring millions into training electricians and skilled workers needed to build their data centres. Google alone has put in $50 million through a partnership with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. BlackRock has chipped in with its own $100 million push to widen training pipelines for its data centers in Texas.

Article Title: Google rolls back satellite image AI tool in less than 24 hours after launch, says: We have also seen people sharing screenshots
Article Text:
Google

What Google said on rolling back the feature



Experts warning to Google on Google Earth feature



In less than a day after Google unveiled a new feature that allowed users to create AI-generated satellite images with the click of a button on its Google Earth platform, the company announced it was removing the tool. Google has rolled back the new feature that allowed Google Earth users to generate AI visualizations on top of the service's satellite imagery. The roll back comes in lass than 24 hours after concerns from researchers and open-source intelligence experts about disinformation risks that the feature raised. The "create image" tool, rolled out Thursday (July 30), integrates Google's Nano Banana 2 image-generation technology to let users zoom into locations and build images in seconds based on Google Earth satellite, aerial and 3D-mapping data.In its initial announcement of the new feature on Thursday, the company said it was designed to work with users' imaginations: "Just zoom in to a place in Google Earth on web (sic), tap 'create image,' and type whatever you want to see," Bryan Horowitz, a product manager wrote.In a statement announcing the company's decision to pause the feature, Google said, "We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world.We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies. So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails. It's important to note that generated images didn’t appear in the main Google Earth experience for others to see and were watermarked as AI generated."Raising alarm on the feature, Henk van Ess, an open-source researcher, wrote on X, "I tried refugees at the Mexican border, a nuclear plant in Iran, a crash in Amsterdam, a hospital with a bomb crater in Gaza. Nothing was refused." Brady Africk, a research analyst at the American Enterprise Institute specializing in satellite imagery analysis, told AFP the Google Earth update "makes it easier to generate convincing fake satellite imagery that can spread quickly online and mislead the public. " "These AI-generated fakes, growing more common, may also erode public trust in satellite imagery, and make the jobs of journalists and researchers more difficult."In a response to AFP and Ess on X, Google said that the images created with the feature include SynthID digital watermarks, invisible markers embedded in media generated using the company's artificial intelligence tools. Users can ask Google's Gemini chatbot if a SynthID is present. "We take misinformation seriously – every image created with Nano Banana in Google Earth includes the SynthID digital watermark, so if someone is unsure about an image, they can ask the Gemini app or use Lens in Search to see if the image was AI-generated. In addition, we prevent image creation on harmful topics and are continually updating our protections," wrote Google.
Article Summary: Google has rolled back a new feature that allowed Google Earth users to generate AI visualizations on top of the service's satellite imagery. The roll back comes in lass than 24 hours after concerns from researchers and open-source intelligence experts about disinformation risks. Google said that the images created with the feature include SynthID digital watermarks.

Article Title: When a district in Florida's Everglades used robot rabbits to eliminate its ever-growing population of Burmese pythons
Article Text:
Image credit: Florida Phyton Challenge website

"Scientists from the South Florida Water Management District (District) and the University of Florida have teamed up to use robotic rabbit decoys as part of our continuing efforts to combat and remove invasive pythons."

How AI-powered robot rabbits work



Why Florida is targeting Burmese pythons



How the robot rabbits complements annual python hunt



"These innovative robots produce a heat signature and emit a smell designed to attract pythons. The robots are equipped with cameras that monitor for pythons and notify District officials when a snake is detected. Once notified, the District can dispatch a python removal agent to the area,”

Florida held its annual Python Challenge just a few weeks ago. The 10-day competition brings together professional and amateur hunters to track and remove invasive Burmese pythons from the Everglades, with cash prizes awarded for capturing the most snakes and the longest python. While the event remains one of the state's biggest efforts to control the invasive species, officials are increasingly turning to technology to find snakes that often remain hidden, and the state continues to battle its growing population of Burmese pythons.Last year, the South Florida Water Management District turned to an unusual technology after the annual Florida Python Challenge: solar-powered robot rabbits. Explaining the initiative, the district said in 2025,Designed to mimic real rabbits using artificial intelligence (AI), heat-signature and scent-simulation technologies, the devices lure pythons out of hiding and alert officials when a snake is detected.Unlike traditional wildlife monitoring tools, the robotic rabbits are designed to imitate real prey. The solar-powered, remote-controlled devices produce both a heat signature and a scent intended to attract Burmese pythons, which rely on thermal sensing and smell while hunting.Each robot is equipped with an AI-powered camera that continuously monitors its surroundings. When the system detects a python approaching, it automatically alerts officials at the South Florida Water Management District. A trained python removal agent is then dispatched to capture and remove the snake.According to the district, the robots are strategically deployed across South Florida at locations where pythons are known to hide, allowing officials to monitor areas that are otherwise difficult to survey.The robot rabbits are the latest addition to Florida's long-running efforts to control Burmese pythons, which were introduced into the wild decades ago and have become one of the Everglades' dominant invasive predators.Conservationists estimate there are between 100,000 and 300,000 Burmese pythons across Florida's subtropical regions. Adult females can lay more than 70 eggs in a single clutch, while the snakes can grow to more than 18 feet long.According to the South Florida Water Management District, invasive pythons prey on native mammals, birds and reptiles, reducing food sources for species including Florida panthers, bobcats and birds of prey.The impact has been documented by the US Geological Survey, whose 2012 study found raccoon and opossum populations in parts of the Everglades had declined by nearly 99% following the spread of Burmese pythons.Before deploying robotic rabbits, Florida primarily relied on trained contractors and public participation through the annual Florida Python Challenge.The 10-day competition brings together professional and amateur snake hunters to remove invasive pythons from the Everglades. Participants must complete a safety course before taking part, and all captured snakes must be euthanised using methods approved by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.More than 600 people had registered for this year’s challenge before it began, while over 900 local and international competitors participated in this year's event.According to the South Florida Water Management District, more than 19,000 Burmese pythons have been removed from the Everglades since 2000 through state removal programmes and public initiatives. Last year, the district said the robotic rabbit programme is intended to complement those efforts rather than replace them.the district noted.
Article Summary: The robots are equipped with cameras that monitor for pythons and notify officials when a snake is detected. The solar-powered, remote-controlled devices produce both a heat signature and a scent intended to attract Burmese python. When the system detects a python approaching, it automatically alerts officials at the South Florida Water Management District.

And I think that's, I think that's wrong. As a country, as a society, as a species, we have proven over and over and over again that we can have safety and privacy."

Cameras targeted across multiple US states

Americans across the country are vandalising surveillance cameras made by Flock Safety. Incidents have been reported from Florida to California amid growing concerns over privacy and government surveillance. The backlash has also reached city governments, with several US cities deactivating the cameras or cancelling contracts with the company.The opposition cuts across political lines. Critics argue the nationwide camera network infringes on personal privacy, while Flock maintains that its technology is designed to improve public safety.said Caleb Williams, a 24-year-old from South Carolina. Responding to the criticism, Flock CEO Garrett Langley told CNN,According to The Guardian, people have cut down Flock cameras with electric saws in New York, thrown paint on them in Oakland, California, rammed vehicles into them in Idaho and physically blocked their view in Florida.The opposition has also reached local governments. Cities including Fort Collins, Colorado; Eugene, Oregon; Madison, Wisconsin; Knoxville, Tennessee; Syracuse, New York; and Walla Walla, Washington, have either deactivated Flock cameras or ended agreements with the company.Flock says it has deployed about 120,000 automated license plate reader (ALPR) and pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) cameras across the United States. The system captures tens of billions of vehicle data points every month, allowing participating law enforcement agencies to search vehicle movements across jurisdictions.The opposition to Flock's surveillance network has brought together people with different political views.said Adrien Kaiser, who described himself as a constitutional conservative.said Jon Dendy, a progressive from Massachusetts.Kaiser said both conservatives and progressives are reaching similar conclusions through different perspectives.he said.The debate has intensified following reports that some police officers used Flock's system to monitor former partners and colleagues. Journalists have also reported that, despite the company's statements that it tracks vehicles rather than people, the system can be used to search for individuals using descriptive information.According to 404 Media, a Flock feature calledallows searches using characteristics such as clothing, tattoos or race. The publication also reported that some police officers conducted searches to assist immigration enforcement.Flock told 404 Media that FreeForm includeswhich alert administrators when search terms includeThe company has also said it does not share its data directly with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Langley said Flock has introduced an automated audit process that flags suspicious searches for administrator review.Privacy advocates say Flock differs from traditional security cameras because its connected network allows law enforcement agencies to search vehicle movements nationwide.said Dave Maass, director of investigations at the Electronic Frontier Foundation.The system has also faced questions over accuracy. In June, automotive journalist Joel Feder said he was stopped by police in Minnesota after a Flock camera incorrectly identified the dealer plate on a Range Rover he was test-driving as matching a stolen vehicle report. Similar concerns over Flock's license plate recognition accuracy have also been reported elsewhere.According to Feder, officers later determined that a similar plate number had been entered incorrectly into the FBI's National Crime Information Center database, which Flock uses for alerts. Langley later described the incident as anand said the underlying federal database was the larger issue.While Flock remains at the centre of the current debate, privacy advocates note that other companies, including Motorola, Vigilant Solutions and Axon, also operate connected license plate recognition systems, suggesting the broader discussion extends beyond a single surveillance provider.
Article Summary: Flock Safety has deployed about 120,000 automated license plate reader (ALPR) and pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) cameras across the United States. The system captures tens of billions of vehicle data points every month, allowing participating law enforcement agencies to search vehicle movements across jurisdictions. Critics argue the nationwide camera network infringes on personal privacy, while Flock maintains that its technology is designed to improve public safety.

Article Title: In 1599, this foundry started making church bells; now it's using 3D printing to preserve 400 year old tradition
Article Text:
Image credit: X (Twitter)

"Certain things are just like they were 400 years ago. But we innovated a lot. Especially within the last 20 years, we've changed a lot."

Traditional casting meets modern technology

Precision remains essential during casting

"The important thing is that you have to calculate, form and then cast the bell as a musical instrument,"

Rising costs and changing demand

"That's why I can't even say how much a bell is going to cost in a year. I just hope the metal price is going to come down again,"

Restoration work helps preserve the craft

"This bell is for the church in Zethau, in Germany. I'm very happy with the casting. I'm especially happy that the innovations of the past decades helped a lot to make the bells ever more beautiful and better,”

One of Europe's last surviving bell foundries is combining centuries-old craftsmanship with modern technologies to keep a tradition dating back more than 400 years alive. At the Grassmayr Bell Foundry in Innsbruck, Austria, artisans continue to cast bronze church bells using techniques passed down through generations, while also relying on 3D printing, laser technology and computer simulations to improve production.Founded in 1599, the family-run foundry is now managed by brothers Johannes and Peter Grassmayr. Explaining how the business has evolved, Johannes Grassmayr told the news agency AP,Workers at the foundry wear protective equipment as they pour molten bronze into specially designed moulds reinforced with steel bands to produce bells weighing several tonnes. The current production includes 12 bells destined for churches in Italy, Germany and Romania.While the overall production cycle still takes three to four months, technology has shortened several stages of the process. According to Johannes Grassmayr, cleaning and polishing a newly cast bell once accounted for nearly 30% of production time. With modern equipment, the same work now takes about one-tenth as long.The foundry also uses technologies including 3D printing, 3D scanning, laser systems, and specialised computer applications to calculate the sound characteristics of each bell. Some production techniques, including a high-pressure sandblasting chamber used for cleaning, remain proprietary.Despite technological advances, creating the mould for a large bell can still take up to six months.Johannes said, adding that the greatest challenge is ensuring the mould withstands the pressure created during casting.According to the foundry, molten bronze inside a mould for a multi-tonne bell can generate up to 125 metric tonnes of pressure. To withstand those forces, workers use high-quality clay moulds enclosed within specially designed steel sleeves.The foundry is also facing business challenges beyond manufacturing. Johannes Grassmayr said demand has been affected as fewer churches are being built across Europe. At the same time, energy prices have increased following the war in Ukraine, while labour costs have risen by around 30% since the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.Material costs have also climbed sharply. According to Johannes, the price of bronze, which is made from 80% copper and 20% tin, has increased from about 8 euros per kilogram a few years ago to around 23 euros per kilogram today.he said.To adapt to changing demand, the Grassmayr family has expanded its restoration business, repairing defective bells using modern technology. According to the company, it has restored hundreds of bells from 12 European countries.Grassmayr bells are installed in more than 100 countries. Among the foundry's largest projects is a bell cast in 2016 for Romania's National Cathedral in Bucharest, measuring 3.3 metres tall and weighing more than 25 metric tonnes. Another 15-metric-tonne bell hangs in a church on Mount Tabor in Israel.Showing recently cast bells cooling inside their moulds, Johannes pointed to the detailed imprint left in the clay.he said.
Article Summary: Grassmayr Bell Foundry in Innsbruck, Austria, was founded in 1599. Artisans continue to cast bronze church bells using techniques passed down through generations. The foundry also uses 3D printing, laser technology and computer simulations to improve production.

Article Title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he got addicted to this ‘Larry Ellison’s app’; It got ‘too powerful’ for him
Article Text:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman compared the experience to a drug

TikTok ownership change in the US

The rise and fall of OpenAI's Sora app

Even Sam Altman is not immune to the endless scrolling on TikTok. The OpenAI CEO recently revealed that he forced himself to get “addicted” to TikTok to study its mechanics only to delete the app after finding it “too powerful” to control. Speaking on a recent episode of the Relentless podcast, Altman shared how a research experiment to understand TikTok’s recommendation algorithm quickly spiraled into a personal distraction.“I made myself get addicted to TikTok, because I wanted to just learn. I really thought it was great. “And then I thought I could control it. I was like, 'Oh, it's actually kind of fun,' but I only use it for 10 minutes to wind down before bed, and I'm totally in control of it. And then it was an hour one night. And then some Saturday afternoon, I was on the couch for like three hours,” Altman said.Altman compared the experience to a drug, noting that while he was “really enjoying it in the moment,” he knew the habit was bad for him. After briefly scaling his usage down to a few minutes before bed, he decided to delete the app entirely.“I briefly got it back under control, and I was down to five, 10 minutes a night, whatever, like a little wind down before bed,” he said, adding, “Then I was just like, enough.”After years of deliberation, TikTok’s US operations are now owned by a majority-investor entity called TikTok USDS Joint Venture that includes Larry Ellison’s Oracle, Silver Lake and MGX. The global operations, however, remain tied to ByteDance, which retains a minority 19.9% share in the US venture. Meanwhile, the storage and algorithmic operations in the US are hosted securely on Oracle cloud infrastructure.Altman’s deep dive into TikTok coincided with OpenAI’s internal efforts to build its own AI-generated video social media platform, Sora. Despite generating massive hype and securing a partnership with Disney, OpenAI officially scrapped the Sora app project in March after six months of development.Company executives determined that rendering video consumed too much computing power at a time when resources were better spent competing with rivals like Anthropic in the core generative AI race.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he got addicted to TikTok to study its mechanics. Altman compared the experience to a drug, noting that while he was “really enjoying it in the moment,” he knew the habit was bad for him. After briefly scaling his usage down, he decided to delete the app entirely.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg is not convinced if OpenAI and Anthropic really want Chinese AI models in America, says: Signal is ...
Article Text:
The increasing Chinese competition



Open vs closed models



Mark Zuckerberg makes an offer to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei



Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has entered the intensifying Washington debate over whether Chinese AI models should be restricted in the US, wanting that banning them would not be ‘an effective solution’. In an interview with Financial Times, Zuckerberg said the US should compete by identifying bottlenecks and roadblocks rather than blocking rivals outright. He also cautioned against ‘regulatory capture’ by American frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which he suggested could use policy to throttle domestic competition. Zuckerberg’s remarks appeared to be a broadside against OpenAI and Anthropic, which dominate the chatbot market with proprietary closed models. He said there were “mixed signals” about whether frontier labs truly want open-source models to succeed. “Are the frontier labs going to want an open-source model to succeed? I think that there have kind of been some mixed signals on that,” he told the FT.The comments from Zuckerberg comes after Beijing-based Moonsht AI released its Kimi K3 model, whose capabilities are nearing those of OpenAI and Anthropic. US officials have also accused Moonshot of covertly training its model using distillation from American rivals, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warning that sanctions are on the table for labs that cross into intellectual property theft.Zuckerberg reiterated his support for “AI for everyone” and open models that users can customize and run on their own hardware — a popular approach among Chinese developers. He warned that AI risks becoming centralized in the hands of a few powerful groups. While Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for stronger regulation and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis has proposed a self-regulatory body, Zuckerberg said restrictions on powerful tools were not the right answer. He argued that open models could help patch cybersecurity vulnerabilities faster than closed ones.Zuckerberg’s intervention highlights a growing split among U.S. tech leaders over how to respond to Chinese competition and regulate AI. While rivals push for tighter controls, he is positioning Meta as a champion of open-source approaches — even as his company develops its own closed model, Muse Spark, citing safety concerns.In related news, recently it was reported that Meta is in early talks to lease computing power to Anthropic in a deal that could be worth as much as $10 billion over two years, according to a New York Times report. If it closes, it would hand Mark Zuckerberg a brand-new line of business and pull Dario Amodei's AI lab deeper into a scramble for compute that shows no sign of easing.The move borrows straight from Elon Musk's playbook. Musk turned SpaceX's Colossus data centers into a rental business earlier this year, and Anthropic became its anchor tenant. Now Zuckerberg wants a slice of the same action, using the very data centers his investors keep grumbling about. Anthropic pitched the idea first, in JuneThe NYT reports that Anthropic proposed the deal in June, and Meta is weighing it. Anthropic would pay in monthly instalments across two years, with either side free to opt out early. The specifics are still moving around.
Article Summary: Zuckerberg says US should compete by identifying bottlenecks and roadblocks rather than blocking rivals outright. Warns against ‘regulatory capture’ by American frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which he suggested could use policy to throttle domestic competition.

Article Title: As AI cracks airlines' 'secret sauce', days of cheap air tickets are over
Article Text:
Representative Image

"secret sauce"

"Consumers should expect that airlines will be smarter about their pricing,"

"exploit that capability to raise fares where possible and cut prices where they have room to stimulate demand.”

How AI is changing airlines ticket prices

Airlines say AI analyses hundreds of variables

"Our models analyse dozens if not hundreds of classes of variables to come up with fares. You can only now do that because of AI,"

Regulators are examining personalised pricing concerns

"surveillance pricing,"

Finding cheap airfares on a busy route may become increasingly difficult as airlines reportedly hand over more of their pricing to artificial intelligence (AI). Instead of relying on fixed pricing rules, carriers are using AI models that analyse demand in real time, reducing the pricing gaps that once helped travellers find lower fares.According to a Bloomberg report, industry executives and analysts have claimed that AI is helping airlines crack the industry's long-held pricingby continuously adjusting fares based on dozens of factors.Bryan Terry of Alton Aviation Consultancy told Bloomberg, adding that airlines willTraditionally, airlines relied on analysts and fixed pricing rules, such as increasing fares after a certain percentage of seats had been sold. According to Bloomberg, AI has replaced many of those manual processes with models that evaluate dozens of variables in real time and continuously adjust ticket prices based on demand.As a result, airlines are selling fewer seats below what they estimate passengers are willing to pay while aiming to fill more seats on each flight.Carriers including Delta Air Lines and Virgin Atlantic have adopted AI-powered pricing tools as part of this shift.The technology does not always lead to higher prices. On routes with weaker demand, AI models can reduce fares to attract more bookings and improve aircraft occupancy.Israeli startup Fetcherr is among the companies developing AI pricing platforms for airlines. Its technology is used by nearly a dozen carriers, including WestJet and Azul.Fetcherr co-founder Uri Yerushalmi told Bloomberg.The company says its technology increases revenue primarily by filling more seats rather than simply raising ticket prices. During recent disruptions in the Middle East, its platform adjusted fares globally in response to oil price movements, cancellations and changing travel demand.AI is also being used after tickets are sold. Volantio, whose software is used by Japan Airlines, identifies passengers who may be willing to switch from full flights in exchange for travel vouchers. Airlines can then resell those seats to last-minute travellers willing to pay higher fares.Consumer groups and lawmakers have raised concerns that AI could eventually enablewhere travellers are charged different fares for the same seat based on personal data such as browsing history or income.According to Simple Flying, the US Federal Trade Commission has opened a civil investigation into whether airlines are using individualised customer data to increase prices. Maryland has also passed the Protection from Predatory Pricing Act, while regulators in other markets have begun examining similar concerns.Airlines and technology providers say their current systems do not use personal information to set ticket prices. Delta has publicly denied using personal data to price fares, while Fetcherr says its models rely on aggregated market data. Volantio has also said its offers are not personalised.While AI may lower fares on less popular routes, analysts say the technology is making airline pricing more responsive to demand, reducing the chances of finding unusually cheap tickets on high-demand flights.

Tech giants Google , Amazon, Microsoft and Meta have cumulatively poured more than $1 trillion into capital investments since the race for artificial intelligence (AI) dominance kicked off three and a half years ago. Driven by escalating projections from Google and Amazon, the four companies plan to spend an additional $745 billion this year, primarily on specialised data centres, advanced semiconductors and the power capacity required to run them.The report says that the combined free cash flow for the four tech giants fell to a decade-low of just $7 billion in the recent quarter, with only Microsoft and Meta bringing in more cash than they spent. Google even recorded its first quarter of negative free cash flow since going public over two decades ago, posting a negative $6 billion for the period.Rishi Jaluria, an RBC Capital analyst, noted that there is essentially no end in sight for capex growth, adding that investors need these firms to toe a tight line between funding AI and preserving the profitability that made them successful in the first place.The scale of long-term financial obligations is expanding rapidly. Google added $500 billion in future financial commitments linked to long-term infrastructure and data center energy deals.Meta signed $233 billion in new commitments, including $96 billion in data centre leases, $112 billion in cloud capacity purchases, and another $68 billion in leases added in July. As per Dec Mullarkey, managing director at SLC Management, investors no longer accept growth at any cost and want to see spending flow directly into financial results.The massive capital rotation is also straining global supply chains. A severe shortage of memory chips has driven up hardware costs across the tech sector, impacting companies like Apple even as it sits outside the central cloud infrastructure battle.

Article Title: US senators send an open letter to Apple CEO Tim Cook; say: We urge Apple to abandon any effort to...
Article Text:
Tim Cook's memory chip problem now has a Senate deadline

Apple's memory chip shortage explained: why MacBook and iPad prices went up 20%

Apple vs YMTC in 2022: the failed Chinese memory chip deal that shaped this letter

Micron's $250 billion US expansion and SK Hynix's Indiana plant are what's at stake

A bipartisan group of US senators has written to Apple CEO Tim Cook asking the company to walk away from Chinese memory chips altogether—not just in devices sold in America, but in every Apple product sold anywhere in the world. The letter, led by New York Democrat Chuck Schumer and Indiana Republican Jim Banks, names two suppliers: ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC). Both sit on the Pentagon's 1260H list of Chinese military companies. Both were reinstated on that list last month after briefly vanishing from it in February, a disappearance that reportedly annoyed the White House enough to get them put back.The senators want Cook to commit, in writing, that neither supplier's memory will end up inside an Apple device. They have given him until August 21 to respond, along with seven questions that go well past a simple yes or no—including what Apple has shown CXMT about its product roadmaps during qualification, and what physical access Chinese engineers would get to Apple's design and supplier-management facilities.Joining Schumer and Banks are Mike Crapo, James Risch, Pete Ricketts, Andy Kim and Jeanne Shaheen.Because RAM has become the most expensive thing in a laptop. AI data centres have swallowed the world's memory supply, DRAM contract prices have roughly quadrupled in a year, and Micron's gross margin has climbed past 80%—a number Apple has been pointing at loudly in Washington. In June, Apple raised MacBook and iPad prices by around 20%. The market took $263 billion off its valuation in a day.Cook addressed it directly in company’s Q3 2026 earnings call, his last as CEO before John Ternus takes over on September 1. Apple raised prices reluctantly, he said, because the industry is in a hundred-year flood on memory pricing. He also noted that three companies—Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung—effectively own DRAM, said more suppliers would help on both supply and price, and added that Apple is evaluating all options. Read alongside the senators' letter, that last line is doing a lot of work.Apple has been here before. Four years ago it had already done the engineering work to qualify YMTC NAND for iPhones sold in China. Word got out, Congress objected, Marco Rubio—then a senator, now Secretary of State—said Apple was playing with fire, and the Biden administration put YMTC on the Commerce Department's Entity List. The deal died.The senators lean on that history hard. Their argument is that the China-only limit will not survive contact with procurement reality: once a part passes Apple's qualification process, shipping it worldwide is one decision away. Apple's own ask appears to have widened along exactly those lines—what began as a China-only request has reportedly grown to cover products sold everywhere. The senators also push back on the cost logic, citing analysis that CXMT's prices are in some cases higher than its global rivals, and that it has already raised prices on existing customers. CXMT only turned profitable after the shortage began, having burned state capital through years of losses. It listed in Shanghai this week seeking $9.8 billion.Follow the states. Schumer is from New York, Banks and Crapo and Risch from Indiana and Idaho—precisely where Micron and SK Hynix are spending the money. Micron has committed $250 billion across New York, Idaho and Virginia, targeting 90,000 jobs and 40% of its DRAM output made in America. SK Hynix is putting roughly $4 billion into an advanced packaging plant next to Purdue University in West Lafayette. Cheap subsidised Chinese memory landing in the middle of that build-out is the outcome these senators are trying to prevent.Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra has been lobbying Lutnick and other officials directly, warning that Chinese memory could hollow out US chipmaking the way subsidised Chinese steel did. The friction is personal too—WSJ reports bad blood dating to Mehrotra's SanDisk years, when he largely avoided meeting Apple.There is also a legal deadline nobody can negotiate around. Section 5949 of the FY2023 NDAA—a Schumer provision—bars federal agencies from buying products containing CXMT or YMTC chips starting December 2027. Apple would be qualifying a supply chain the US government is already required to phase out.Apple has not commented on the letter. Trump meets Chinese Premier Xi Jinping in the US in September, with export controls on the agenda.
Article Summary: US senators want Apple to stop using Chinese memory chips in all its products. They want Tim Cook to commit that neither supplier's memory will end up inside an Apple device. They have given him until August 21 to respond, along with seven questions that go well past a simple yes or no.

Article Title: PwC's US CEO to companies: Stop thinking AI can fix your broken business, all AI is going to do for you is tell you how bad your…
Article Text:
PwC US CEO Paul Griggs: AI won't fix a broken business, it will just expose it

PwC CEO says AI adoption fails when it is handed to the CIO and treated as an IT project

Paul Griggs is running the same AI playbook inside PwC, from billable hours to partner headcount

PwC US CEO Paul Griggs has a blunt warning for companies writing large cheques for AI: the technology will not rescue a business that is already running badly. Speaking to Business Insider, Griggs said firms that bolt AI onto inefficient workflows end up in the same place they started, only with a costlier version of the problem. His line on it was direct—if you layer AI on messy processes, it will only show you how messy they are.That was one of two misconceptions Griggs flagged. The other is structural, and he thinks it explains why so many AI rollouts stall before they show a return. Companies keep filing AI under technology, when the work is really about people, processes and the willingness to rebuild both.Griggs told Business Insider that firms viewing AI as a tech transformation will keep tripping over the same obstacles. When the mandate sits entirely with the CIO or CTO, he said, the organisation is missing the opportunity. His framing instead: a large-scale business transformation, and a change-management exercise that touches every employee and every process.The fix, in his view, is end-to-end. Rebuild the workflow first, then work out which parts of it actually benefit from the technology. Customer relationships and new revenue lines matter as much as the software.The advice is not theoretical for him. Griggs told the Financial Times in March that PwC partners unwilling to be AI-first would eventually be replaced, and that nobody at the firm gets an exemption. PwC has since moved to loosen its dependence on billing by the hour, launching a platform called PwC One that packages services like M&A due diligence and tax guidance into automated tools clients can use with no PwC staffer involved, priced by subscription or consumption. Hiring has tilted toward engineers and data specialists over traditional accountants and consultants.Griggs joined the Big Four firm as an intern roughly 30 years ago and calls AI the biggest opportunity of his career. Taking the productivity savings straight to the bottom line, though, is what he called the lazy answer. The harder question is whether leadership will spend that dividend on growth instead of pocketing it.
Article Summary: PwC US CEO Paul Griggs: AI won't fix a broken business, it will just expose it. He says firms that bolt AI onto inefficient workflows end up in the same place they started, only with a costlier version of the problem. The fix, in his view, is end-to-end. Rebuild the workflow first, then work out which parts of it actually benefit from the technology.

Article Title: US government plans $100,000 fee on foreign students: What it means for engineers and others planning to work in US
Article Text:
Representiative image

What is actually being proposed for foreign students and hopeful engineers



$100,000 fee is not a standalone move



Why Indian students and freshers are exposed



The US government is reportedly weighing $100,000 fee on foreign students who want to work after graduating. For a generation of Indian engineers already impacted by September’s H-1B hike, the American dream appears to be slipping further away. For years, the promise was simple: get into a good American university, work hard, land a job and the rest would eventually follow. That promise is now looking shakier than it has in decades.According to a report by the Wall Street Journal, the Trump administration is weighing a $100,000 fee on international students who want to work in the US after they graduate. The fee would attach to Optional Practical Training, or OPT, which is the program that lets international graduates work in the US for one to three years on their student visa, often as the first real step toward a longer-term career and eventual H-1B sponsorship.Data shows that roughly 419,000 people were working under OPT in 2024. If this fee is enacted, most of them and those hoping to follow in their footsteps would be pricing themselves out of that option entirely. A DHS spokeswoman said no policy should be considered final until formally announced, but the direction of travel is hard to miss.To understand why this lands hard, let us rewind to September. Last year, President Trump signed an order imposing a $100,000 annual fee on companies sponsoring H-1B visas – the visa category that lets skilled foreign workers stay in the US long-term.That fee alone marked a jump of more than 10,000% from what companies used to pay (a combined $995 in lottery and petition fees).The scale of that increase sent tech and finance firms into a scramble: Microsoft, JPMorgan and Amazon all sent internal emails urging H-1B holders to stay in the US or return immediately before the new rule kicked in at midnight on September 20, with one law firm advising JPMorgan staff to avoid international travel entirely until the government offered clearer guidance.The two fees target different stages of the same pipeline. The H-1B fee hit people already employed and sponsored. The proposed OPT fee would hit the stage before that to new graduates who haven’t even gotten a job offer yet, let alone sponsorship.The numbers make clear who absorbs most of this. Citing government data, news agency Reuters reported in September that Indians accounted for 71% of all approved H-1B visas last year, with China a distant second at 11.7%. Companies like Amazon (over 12,000 H-1B approvals in the first half of 2025), along with Microsoft and Meta (over 5,000 each), lean heavily on this talent pipeline.For a student who has already spent years and often a family’s life savings on a US degree, betting on OPT, a $100,000 price tag before they’ve even earned their first paycheque changes the math completely. Recent graduates and early-career engineers in more routine technical roles are the most exposed — the ones without years of specialised experience to justify a company absorbing that cost.Meanwhile, with $100,000 H1-B fees, startups and smaller firms, which have long been an entry point for younger international talent, may simply stop sponsoring altogether. What’s left standing is a narrower path that only senior engineers, researchers and highly specialised professionals can realistically walk through.
Article Summary: The fee would attach to Optional Practical Training, or OPT, which is the program that lets international graduates work in the US for one to three years. Data shows that roughly 419,000 people were working under OPT in 2024. A DHS spokeswoman said no policy should be considered final until formally announced, but the direction of travel is hard to miss.

Article Title: While 'drama' surrounding Warren Buffett's donation to Gates Foundation is over, there’s new debate on his $140 billion ‘gift’
Article Text:
Warren Buffet (File photo)

“gift"

Tax benefits exist, but experts say they are not the central issue

"They spend more like operating charities than endowments,"

"It isn't fair to accuse [Buffett] of warehousing his funds,"

"The alternative to a disclosed, floor-bound vehicle usually isn't more democratic giving,"

"It's less accountable giving."

Warren Buffett’s $140 billionto his children's charitable foundations is facing criticism. This comes after the recentsurrounding the legendary investor's decision to stop the long-running tradition of directing his annual Berkshire Hathaway share donations to the Gates Foundation and instead channel his fortune to foundations run by his children. According to CNBC, some readers questioned whether the move was intended to avoid taxes or to slow the flow of money to nonprofits.Whereas gifts of appreciated stock by rich individuals were already enjoying tax advantages, experts told Fortune that the recent decision made by Buffett has revived concerns regarding how one should evaluate the efforts of billionaires in philanthropy based on tax deductions or based on the promptness of getting money to charity organisations. These experts say it is all about how Buffett has structured his philanthropic efforts, specifically whether he chose a vehicle that provides accountability and the prompt distribution of funds to charities.According to Allison Tait, a law professor at the University of Richmond who studies wealth transfer, donating appreciated stock instead of selling it removes the shares from a donor's taxable estate and avoids capital gains taxes that would otherwise apply after a sale.Tait told Fortune.She estimated that Buffett could avoid between $33 billion and $56 billion in taxes by transferring his Berkshire Hathaway shares to family foundations rather than selling them first.The discussion has also highlighted an apparent contrast with Buffett's longstanding public support for stronger estate taxes. During testimony before the US Senate Finance Committee in 2007, Buffett warned thatadding thatTait said Buffett would likely argue that he is using the current tax rules while continuing to advocate for legislative changes. However, she added that avoiding taxes on this scale raises questions alongside his calls for reform.Jane Ditelberg, chief tax strategist at Northern Trust Wealth Management, told Fortune that charitable gifts of appreciated securities have long received favourable tax treatment because charities themselves are tax-exempt.Ditelberg said.Experts also noted that recent US tax law changes do not support claims that Buffett accelerated the transfers to avoid future changes to estate taxes. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in July 2025, permanently raised the federal estate tax exemption to $15 million per individual, reducing any urgency to make immediate transfers, according to Janetta Cravens, founder of CoSpire Consulting.Experts told Fortune that the more significant distinction lies in the type of charitable vehicle used to distribute wealth. Private foundations, such as those run by Buffett's family, must publicly disclose their grants through annual tax filings and distribute at least 5% of their assets each year. Critics argue that this minimum payout allows foundations to retain large endowments for extended periods while meeting only the legal requirement.However, Jack Lewars, founder of Ultra Philanthropy, said Buffett's family foundations distribute substantially more than the minimum. According to Inside Philanthropy, the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation has averaged payouts of about 41% over five years, while the Howard G. Buffett Foundation and Sherwood Foundation have averaged approximately 59% and 87%, respectively.Lewars told Fortune, adding that Buffett's previous donations to the Gates Foundation also came with the condition that the funds be spent within the year they were received.Lewars said.Experts contrasted private foundations with donor-advised funds (DAFs), which offer donors immediate tax deductions but have no mandatory annual payout requirements and are not required to publicly disclose grant distributions.Cravens said.The discussion regarding Buffett's recent philanthropic act has therefore shifted from whether he receives any tax benefit, which,, according to experts, is very common under current US law, to whether there is adequate transparency in other forms of charitable organisation.
Article Summary: Warren Buffett’s $140 billionto his children's charitable foundations is facing criticism. Some readers questioned whether the move was intended to avoid taxes or to slow the flow of money to nonprofits. Experts say it is all about how Buffett has structured his philanthropic efforts, specifically whether he chose a vehicle that provides accountability.

Article Text:
Fortitude is a World War II spy thriller starring Nicolas Cage as real-life spy Dusko Popov

Plaintiffs claim film's value has been damaged

Netflix disputes responsibility

Netflix has been sued for $105 million by a UK-based production company and a filmmaker who alleged that the streaming platform lost a hard drive containing a copy of an unreleased World War II espionage film. According to a CBS report, the complaint has been filed in California district court. It alleges that the film's associate producer, Daniel Haido, hand-delivered an unencrypted master copy of the movie “Fortitude” to Netflix for a private screening as the company considered acquiring its distribution rights. The World War II spy thriller stars Nicolas Cage as real-life spy Dusko Popov, along with Sir Ben Kingsley and Ron Perlman.The plaintiffs argue the incident has undermined the film's exclusivity and made potential buyers less likely to purchase it. However, a little more than a week later, Netflix informed the filmmakers that the hard drive had been stolen. “Someone stole a good amount of drives from our office desks this past week,” a Netflix executive wrote in the email, according to the suit.The lawsuit says "Fortitude" took more than seven years to make and cost about $45 million.The filmmakers argue that studios may now avoid buying the film because an unauthorized copy could be released online."The film's value depended in significant part on its exclusivity as an unreleased, first-to-market work," the complaint states. "By losing control of the film, Netflix destroyed that exclusivity and materially, if not completely, impaired the film's marketability."A Netflix spokesperson told CBS News that the company disputes the claims. “Netflix disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards,” the spokesperson told the publication.The company added that it has offered to monitor piracy websites for any unauthorized distribution or sale of the movie. “While we do not own the rights to Fortitude, we take content security seriously and have taken extra measures to support the filmmaker and his team,” the spokesperson said.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei: "I think that most people are underestimating just how radical the upside of AI could be, just as..."
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei

"I think that most people are underestimating just how radical the upside of AI could be, just as I think most people are underestimating how bad the risks could be."

— Dario Amodei



Who is Dario Amodei?

Understanding the quote

Why the quote has attracted attention

The wider debate surrounding artificial intelligence

Why this is today's quote

Artificial intelligence has rapidly moved from research laboratories into everyday life, powering everything from search engines and chatbots to scientific research, software development and medical discoveries. As governments, businesses and researchers race to understand the technology's implications, conversations about AI have become increasingly divided between optimism and caution. Among the voices shaping that debate is Dario Amodei, the co-founder and CEO of Anthropic and a former research leader at OpenAI. Today's Quote of the Day highlights one of his most widely discussed observations on artificial intelligence, a statement that suggests public conversations often underestimate both AI's transformative potential and the scale of the risks that could accompany its rapid advancement. The quote has become one of the defining summaries of Amodei's broader philosophy on the future of AI.The statement appears in Amodei's 2024 essay Machines of Loving Grace, a long-form reflection on how advanced artificial intelligence could reshape society over the coming decades. Rather than presenting a prediction, the essay explores a range of possibilities, arguing that AI has the potential to accelerate scientific discovery, improve healthcare, transform education and raise living standards while also creating challenges that demand careful preparation.Dario Amodei is one of the most influential figures in the field of artificial intelligence. He co-founded Anthropic in 2021 alongside several former OpenAI researchers, including his sister Daniela Amodei. The company has since become one of the leading developers of frontier AI systems, producing the Claude family of language models that compete with products from OpenAI, Google and other major technology firms.Before establishing Anthropic, Amodei served as Vice President of Research at OpenAI, where he played a significant role in the development of large language models, including GPT-2 and GPT-3. Earlier in his career, he worked as a research scientist at Google Brain and has also contributed to influential research on reinforcement learning from human feedback and AI safety.Over the past decade, Amodei has become a prominent voice in discussions surrounding AI capabilities, governance and long-term societal impacts. His work has often focused on ensuring that increasingly capable AI systems are developed with appropriate safeguards while allowing innovation to continue.At first glance, Amodei's statement appears to make two contrasting claims. The first is that artificial intelligence could deliver benefits that exceed current expectations. These benefits may include breakthroughs in medicine, faster scientific discoveries, improvements in education, enhanced productivity and solutions to complex engineering and environmental challenges.The second part of the quote argues that the risks associated with advanced AI may also be underestimated. Those concerns extend beyond technical issues and include broader questions surrounding misinformation, cybersecurity, economic disruption, labour markets, privacy, national security and the governance of increasingly capable AI systems.Taken together, the statement suggests that discussions about AI should avoid reducing the technology to either utopian optimism or dystopian pessimism. Instead, it proposes that both possibilities deserve careful examination because powerful technologies have historically produced significant benefits while also introducing unexpected challenges.Artificial intelligence has become one of the most debated technologies of the modern era. New AI systems are increasingly capable of generating text, images, software code, scientific analyses and creative content that previously required substantial human expertise. As a result, public conversations often alternate between excitement over AI's possibilities and concern over its consequences.Amodei's quote has attracted attention because it resists choosing between these competing narratives. Rather than arguing that AI will either solve humanity's greatest problems or create unprecedented dangers, he suggests that both perspectives may underestimate the scale of what lies ahead.That balanced framing has made the quote one of the most frequently referenced passages from Machines of Loving Grace. It is often cited in discussions involving policymakers, researchers, business leaders and technology companies attempting to understand the pace and direction of AI development.The questions raised by Amodei's quote reflect broader debates taking place across governments, universities and the technology industry.Supporters of advanced AI argue that increasingly capable systems could accelerate research into diseases, improve public services, enhance productivity, assist scientific discovery and expand access to education. AI has already demonstrated its usefulness in fields ranging from drug discovery and weather forecasting to language translation and software engineering.At the same time, researchers and policymakers continue to examine concerns surrounding misinformation, deepfakes, bias in AI systems, intellectual property, job displacement, cybersecurity and the concentration of AI capabilities among a relatively small number of organisations. Several governments have introduced or proposed regulatory frameworks aimed at ensuring transparency, accountability and safety in the development of advanced AI technologies.These discussions have become more prominent as companies continue to release increasingly capable AI models while investing billions of dollars in research and infrastructure.Amodei occupies a distinctive position within the AI industry because he has spent much of his career working on both the technical development of advanced AI systems and the research surrounding their safe deployment. His experience spans academic research, large-scale model development and leadership within one of the world's foremost AI companies.Although his views are not universally shared, they are widely followed because they reflect the perspective of someone directly involved in building frontier AI technologies. His writings and public remarks have contributed to ongoing conversations about AI governance, model evaluation, safety standards and the responsibilities of companies developing increasingly powerful systems.The most enduring quotations often capture complex ideas in a few carefully chosen words. Amodei's observation does exactly that. Rather than encouraging either uncritical enthusiasm or excessive alarm, it highlights the possibility that artificial intelligence could reshape society in ways that are more profound than many people currently anticipate, for better and for worse.Whether readers ultimately agree with his assessment or not, the quote serves as a reminder that discussions about artificial intelligence are unlikely to be settled by simple answers. As AI continues to evolve and become more deeply integrated into everyday life, evaluating its future will require equal attention to its opportunities, its limitations and the responsibilities that accompany technological progress.
Article Summary: Dario Amodei is one of the most influential figures in the field of artificial intelligence. He is the co-founder and CEO of Anthropic and a former research leader at OpenAI. Today's Quote of the Day highlights a statement that suggests public conversations often underestimate both AI's transformative potential and the scale of the risks that could accompany its rapid advancement.

Michael Burry’s ‘bibical’ warning

Article Title: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma lays out four-point plan after 2,800 job cuts: 'We will not live on past successes'
Article Text:
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's post-layoff plan: growth by 2027, 500 million daily players by 2030

Xbox has 100 million daily players and wants half a billion by 2030, which is a very steep hill

The 3% margin problem: why Sony and Nintendo are the numbers Xbox keeps staring at

Minecraft, Candy Crush and Fallout: where Xbox is actually spending money now

Three weeks after beginning the biggest restructuring in Xbox history, Asha Sharma has told her staff where the gaming division goes from here. In a memo sent on Thursday, July 30, obtained by The Verge, the Xbox CEO said the business will return to player and revenue growth by the end of fiscal year 2027, which wraps next June. Profits, she added, need to climb back in line with industry averages. Every function and every studio owns a slice of that outcome.The timing is uncomfortable, and Sharma doesn't pretend otherwise. Microsoft eliminated 1,600 Xbox roles on July 6 and flagged roughly 1,250 more over the following year, with four studios—Double Fine, Compulsion, Ninja Theory and Undead Labs — leaving the fold. Sharma's own July memo put the full FY27 reduction nearer 3,200. Days before this latest note landed, Xbox reported a 10% quarterly revenue slide, its weakest showing since 2022, with annual revenue down $1.7 billion. Microsoft stock, buoyed by cloud and AI, jumped almost 16% anyway.Sharma laid out four priorities for FY27, each starting with the letter C: strengthen the platform led by console, grow games into global franchises, turn Minecraft into a creator platform, and extend the worlds fans already love.Progress gets measured in three stages. Growth returns by mid-2027. FY28 and FY29 are for converting bets into real revenue. By FY30, Xbox wants to be halfway to what Sharma calls its "long-term daily-player goal"—the billion-people-a-day ambition she floated in the reset memo. Xbox currently pulls in more than 100 million people daily, 500 million monthly and close to a billion a year. Getting to 500 million daily inside four years works out to roughly 50% growth annually, which nobody in gaming has done.The profitability gap is the sharper story. Sharma and content chief Matt Booty have said Xbox will end the year around a 3% accountability margin. Sony's game and network services arm posted a 9.9% operating margin last fiscal year. Nintendo's ran close to 16%. Sharma wants parity by next year and wants to be ahead of both by mid-2030.Part of the squeeze is hardware. Console storage component prices have more than doubled twice since Sharma took the job in February, and she expects another jump heading into the 2027 holiday quarter, taking costs past 5x what Microsoft paid two years earlier. Memory has followed a similar curve. Xbox can't build as many consoles as buyers want, which is a strange sentence to write about a struggling platform.The studio system is shifting from a decentralised setup to one built around the strongest franchises and, in Sharma's words, the biggest new ideas. The Fallout push already reflects that. Three Xbox franchises clear $1 billion a year each, though she didn't name them.Expect those to spread outward: film, television, consumer products, sponsorships, live experiences and new global partnerships, China included. For casual gaming share, Xbox leans on King, the Candy Crush studio, plus Microsoft Casual Games. Minecraft gets more investment than it ever has, aimed at creation tools, audience-building and letting players earn.Sharma, who came from Instacart and Meta and replaced Phil Spencer in February, has spent six months cutting Game Pass prices, appointing new leaders and restoring console exclusives—Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution among them. Satya Nadella told analysts this week that Microsoft is making the decisions needed across content, platform and operations to reset gaming for long-term growth.Her July 6 memo ended with a warning about companies that mistake longevity for inevitability. This one opens with a version of the same idea: "We will not live on past successes or be trapped by past failures." The four C's are the plan. FY27 is the proof.
Article Summary: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma laid out four priorities for FY27, each starting with the letter C. Sharma has spent six months cutting Game Pass prices, appointing new leaders and restoring console exclusives. The studio system is shifting from a decentralised setup to one built around the strongest franchises.
